At ten past nine, while the others were presenting, I was reading the file.
Thanks for coming down. Alan Pierce, internal review. This is not about you, and it will take four minutes.
That is fine. I have five before my next call.
Tuesday morning. What were you doing at around ten forty?
I was checking the quarter file at my desk. I had been there since about nine thirty.
And did anything interrupt you?
Yes. While I was working, somebody walked past with a box of files. I glanced up, I did not recall the face, and I went back to the file.
You said around ten forty. The badge log has you back from the coffee area at ten fifty-two. Which one is right?
Then it was after ten fifty-two, and around ten forty was too vague. I would rather correct it now than contradict myself in writing.
I was checking the quarter file when my phone rang.
I would rather correct that now than contradict myself in writing.
While I was working, somebody walked past and I glanced up.
What were you doing when that happened?

The thing people get wrong about memory is that they think of it as a recording. You press play and the afternoon comes back. It is not a recording. Every time you tell a story, you are not replaying the original event, you are rebuilding it out of pieces, and then you save the new version over the old one. So the fifth time you tell it, you are remembering the fourth telling. There is a famous study where people watched the same film of two cars, and half of them were asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other, and the other half were asked how fast they were going when they hit each other. One word. The smashed group gave speeds that were significantly higher. And a week later, when everybody came back, some of the smashed group remembered broken glass on the road. There was no broken glass in that film. Here is the part that matters in a room where somebody is taking notes: confidence tells you almost nothing about accuracy. The most confident witnesses are not the most accurate ones, and that surprises everybody, including the witnesses themselves.

I train people to ask questions for a living, and I have three rules. Rule one. Never open with what somebody saw. Open with what they were doing. It sounds like small talk and it is not: it gives the person a place to stand, and everything else hangs off it. Somebody who tells you they were making coffee at ten will remember far more than somebody you asked, cold, what they saw at ten. Rule two. Treat the word around as a warning light. Around ten almost always means I do not know. Do not ask for the time again, because they will invent one to be helpful, and now you have a wrong time in writing. Ask what else was happening at that moment instead. A phone call, a delivery, the end of a meeting. Those things have records, and the records give you the time for free. Rule three, and this is the one nobody does. After somebody finishes an answer, say nothing for four seconds. Just wait. Most of what I have learned in twenty years arrived in that gap, and none of it would have arrived if I had filled it.
